title: Editorial: Why wine doesn’t begin at 95 points
summary:
In the space of a few days this past July, some of South Africa’s most celebrated producers – Sadie Family Wines, Van Loggerenberg and David & Nadia – released new wines. The post Editorial: Why wine doesn’t begin at 95 points appeared first on winemag.
content:
In the space of a few days this past July, some of South Africa’s most celebrated producers – Sadie Family Wines, Van Loggerenberg and David & Nadia – released new wines. Over the course of the month, 15 wines were awarded 97 points or more on this site. These are genuinely exceptional wines. But when exceptional becomes commonplace, what happens to the meaning of the score?

The wine world has a peculiar relationship with numbers. We claim to appreciate nuance, complexity and individuality, yet we often reduce wines to a single figure.

A 95-point wine is understood to be “better” than a 90-point wine. For many, a 94-point wine is somehow one point short of greatness. A 96-point wine demands attention. A 97-point wine demands acquisition.

But what happens when excellent wines become so plentiful that 95 points no longer separates the truly exceptional from the merely very good?

South Africa is currently producing more outstanding wines than ever before. Vineyard understanding has improved, winemaking has become more thoughtful, and a new generation of producers is crafting wines of remarkable precision and character. The result is a fortunate problem: there are too many good choices.

Which raises a question: are consumers overlooking wines of real character simply because they do not score in the mid-90s?

When excellence becomes widespread, distinction becomes harder. If 15 wines can secure 97 points or higher in a single month, the consumer is left staring at a constellation of high numbers with few navigational tools.

Moreover, the scoring system has its blind spots. A thrilling old-vine Palomino or Colombard can offer rarity, character and a sense of place, yet struggle to reach the mid-90s because it does not conform to the traditional markers of greatness. The Platklip Palomino Old Vine 2025 from Piekenierskloof is a case in point – a wine that gave me much pleasure, but one I could not in good conscience score higher than 93.

There is also a danger that the pursuit of high scores encourages a stylistic consensus. Producers, consciously or otherwise, may gravitate towards the characteristics most consistently rewarded by critics – whether that means power and extraction, or, conversely, extreme reduction, hyper-lean fruit and searing acidity.

As scores climb, so too do the prices attached to benchmark bottles. But does a 98-point wine offer twice the emotional and intellectual reward of a 93-point wine? Rarely. Yet the market treats the numerical gap as a chasm.

When every release is heralded as a “masterpiece” or a “triumph of the vintage,” the language of praise becomes exhausted. Eventually, hyperbole eats its own tail.

The tyranny of the number

Here are some reasons why the growing preoccupation with high scores – and the status they confer – risks narrowing our understanding of what makes a wine important.

The first misconception about wine scores is that they measure how much you will enjoy a wine. They do not.

A score is an assessment of a wine against certain criteria: complexity, balance, intensity, length, typicity, ageing potential and overall quality. It is not a prediction of your personal preference.

A 92-point wine made in a style you love will almost certainly give you more pleasure than a 96-point wine that does not suit your palate. The most important critic remains the person drinking the wine. Some consumers prefer bright, fresh, energetic wines. Others enjoy richness and power. Some want intellectual complexity; others simply want something delicious with dinner. Indeed, even the same person’s preferences legitimately change depending on context, mood and occasion. A score cannot account for all of this.

High-scoring wines are frequently expensive wines. This is understandable. Old vineyards, meticulous farming, limited production and elaborate élevage involving considerable cellar investment all come at a cost.

But the relationship between quality and price is not linear. The difference between a 95-point wine and a 93-point wine may be almost impossible to detect for many consumers, while the price difference can be substantial.

A critic’s most useful recommendation is often not the wine that achieved the highest score, but the wine where quality, character and price intersect most convincingly. A 91-point wine at R150 can be a far more exciting discovery than a 96-point wine at R1,500.

There is a danger that chasing scores turns wine into a trophy-hunting exercise rather than an exploration. I say this with some discomfort, having played my own small part in the 95-point economy. Critics are very much part of the ecosystem that I believe needs to evolve. The highest-scoring wines can become objects of status as much as objects of enjoyment – collected, traded and displayed as markers of taste and access. In this environment, wine risks becoming less about curiosity and pleasure, and more about acquiring the “right” bottles: the rarest, the most expensive, the ones carrying the biggest numbers.

What ever happened to curiosity?

The joy of wine lies partly in finding something unexpected: a producer you have not heard of, a variety you have never tried, a region you have overlooked. Twenty years ago, South Africa’s fine wine consumers were arguably more open-minded and adventurous. The category was still being defined; drinkers were willing to experiment, to follow unfamiliar names and to take a chance on wines that did not yet come with established reputations.

There is a danger that the openness that characterised that era is beginning to narrow. A handful of producers, deservedly admired as they are, have become so firmly entrenched at the top of the wine scene that it becomes harder for newer protagonists to gain attention. The next generation of ambitious producers, or those working with less fashionable varieties and overlooked sites, can struggle to break through.

If every buying decision begins and ends with “What scored highest?”, discovery disappears. And without discovery, wine becomes much less interesting.

The irony is that consumers may need critics more than ever – but perhaps not in the way they once did. The critic’s role is not simply to identify the wines that deserve attention. In an age of abundance, that is no longer enough.

The more valuable role is to provide context. To explain why a wine matters. To identify character and value. To separate the memorable from the merely impressive.

Scores provide a useful common language and a quick reference point. For many consumers, especially those without the time to taste widely, they are an invaluable shortcut. The issue is not their existence, but the weight we attach to them. They should be an invitation to explore, not a reason to stop looking.

There is pleasure in greatness, but there is also pleasure in modesty. Sometimes the most satisfying wine is simply the one that fits the moment. If every bottle we opened had to be “great”, greatness itself would soon lose its meaning.

title: Tim James: Eben Sadie and making wine in the vineyard
summary:
Great wine is made in the vineyard, they say – essentially claiming little more than that you need good grapes for good wine, and the better your grapes the better your wine (as long as you don’t stuff it all up in the winery). Fair enough, but there’s another, more radical way of looking at […]

The post Tim James: Eben Sadie and making wine in the vineyard appeared first on winemag.
content:
Great wine is made in the vineyard, they say – essentially claiming little more than that you need good grapes for good wine, and the better your grapes the better your wine (as long as you don’t stuff it all up in the winery). Fair enough, but there’s another, more radical way of looking at the idea, and Eben Sadie is doing just that, with the multi-varietal wines he makes. The Palladius and Columella blends make for the really complex, fascinating story – one that I think I have come to comprehend, but only recently. A report here, admittedly for the more geekishly inclined.

Let me start the exploration, though, with a few more explanatory words about the two field-blends that I spoke about a few weeks ago when reporting on the latest batch of new releases. Red Songvang and white Twiswind come from two mixed vineyards on the home farm, planted with 12 grapes each (white varieties in the one vineyard, red in the other, obviously). Inevitably they don’t all ripen perfectly at the same time (there does, in fact, seem to be a tendency for such mixed vineyards to start homogenising ripeness  in the longer term). So Eben does two picks in each vineyard, about a week apart, averaging for the earlier- and later-ripening varieties. Then, with no selection except to discard poor quality individual berries, the grapes of the two vineyards will naturally ferment together in their own tanks, and, voilà, the two wines are born and start growing up, heading for the bottle.

As to those youngish vineyards, the plantings in both were informedly experimental. If any of the varieties planted perform somewhat disappointingly or unusefully over the years, they might well be replaced, and, in time, if interplanting is necessary tweaks could be made. The vineyards will evolve, but the concept of expressing the single mixed vineyard will remain: all the varieties unquestioningly accepted and cofermented. Any change to the blend will come from changes in the vineyard.

And so, mutatis mutandis, to the more complexly-treated blends of Palladius (15 varieties off 17 vineyards) and Columella (seven grapes, seven vineyards). I suggested before that they’re perhaps best thought of as field-blends too – with the Swartland serving as an enormous vineyard/tract of terroir to be expressed in all its aspects. A big difference though, is that each of the contributory vineyards is vinified separately. It would be hard to do otherwise but, says Eben, the practice means that the vineyard and how best to manage it can be continuously observed, from year to year (for example, he once came to realise that a particular block was being too heavily composted, with a resultant richness of soil that produced results in the wine that he didn’t want). “I realised”, Eben told me, “that you can’t study a system [that is, Swartland terroir], if you have too many exceptions”.

So, for a year the two sets of wines made from each vineyard mature individually. Then they are blended together according, approximately, to soil type; these going into large foudres for a year – to be further observed – before the final blending is done. I should perhaps say “mixing” rather than “blending”, for the traditional, standard idea of blending wines is for the judicious cellarmaster to sample all the candidate barrels and choose the ones that will make the best wine through quality or character or variety, or perhaps to best continue the established style of the wine. Frequently, as in Bordeaux, the varietal mix of the vineyard is there to allow for the strength of the different varieties in a particular vintage to shine (Cabernet didn’t uniformly ripen, perhaps, but merlot did, or the cab franc performed particularly attractively).

In the Sadie cellar, however, there is no such selection at blending time. There hadn’t even been selection in the vineyards – no picking on two or three different dates to allow for all the grapes to be picked at optimal ripeness; they must all be picked together on the date chosen (a crucial choice, of course). And in the cellar, as I say, no picking and choosing – once the vineyard is picked, its grapes are destined for the final blend and the bottle.

This is a pretty remarkable practice for wines of such ambition (and such reputation and price). Everything is thrown onto the quality of the viticulture, and the selection of vineyards, which of course involves a basic selection of varieties.

Eben has never thought of Columella and Palladius as anything other than works in progress. Over the years they will evolve – primarily through viticultural practice, not in the cellar. We can expect, I think, more vineyards to come into play, rather than any being abandoned while they produce good grapes. Eventually some will die, or need progressive radical interplanting – as is already happening. Some will be tweaked in various ways. Eben tells, for example, of an old chenin vineyard on the home farm that goes into Palladius. He would like more acidity from it, so he’s removing dying or dead vines, replacing them with colombard, clairette and picpoule.

Long ago Eben said to me that “building a great wine is not the work of one generation” – and great Swartland wine is what his ambition and all his efforts are directed towards. He has always serenely accepted that his continuing project will outlast him. More recently he put a slightly different angle on this, talking about what he learns from observing what his component vineyards are offering, year after year, in seasons of different character: “The study of a region”, he says, “is the work of generations”. Even more so in this time of climatic change. Making wine in the vineyard, as done in pre-industrial times, is the hard option.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Jamie Goode: Can terroir survive climate change?
summary:
There’s a lot of discussion about the change in climate. Currently, in the UK, we are in the middle of the hottest summer ever, and the last hottest summer ever was in 2022, just four years ago. It has been like California here: hot and dry, and actually quite pleasant if you like it hot. […]

The post Jamie Goode: Can terroir survive climate change? appeared first on winemag.
content:
There’s a lot of discussion about the change in climate. Currently, in the UK, we are in the middle of the hottest summer ever, and the last hottest summer ever was in 2022, just four years ago. It has been like California here: hot and dry, and actually quite pleasant if you like it hot. But weird, and not the weather usually associated with the UK. Meanwhile, Bordeaux and other more southerly locations have been burning. It’s all a bit apocalyptic.

This brings us round to the notion of terroir. Let’s take Burgundy as an example, which over recent decades has become a place of pilgrimage for wine lovers around the world. In the Parker era, Bordeaux was the pre-eminent wine region; now Parker has stopped and the world has moved away from the somewhat childish tastes of big, ripe, expansive, expensive oak-laden reds and discovered the magic of elegance and place over power, Burgundy is the hallowed ground that wine lovers trek to with reverence and longing.

There are 1,247 climats in Burgundy, on a patchwork of vineyards that threads along 60 km of gentle slopes, running from Dijon to the south of Beaune. These are patches of land recognized as individual terroir units, and together with the hierarchical classification of regional, village, premier cru and grand cru, we have this most beautifully organized presentation of terroir in the world. The status of each parcel tallies well with the soil and underlying geology, as well as the place on the slope. The climats achieved UNESCO world heritage status in 2015.

And these patches of land are then interpreted almost exclusively through the lens of two grape varities: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

But with the change in climate, which has been chaotic, but which has had a clear warming trend, there’s worry that these two remarkable varieties may no longer be faithful conduits of terroir in Burgundy. The fear is that when the climate is changed, the hard work that has led to the identification of these terroirs will begin to unravel.

The theory behind this is that there are windows of terroir expression in terms of grape ripeness. The signal of terroir is lost if the grapes are picked too early, or too late; it is also lost if there is too much ripeness in the grapes, even if they are picked at the right time.

With a warmer climate, there may be vintages where Burgundy from top sites just tastes like good Pinot Noir or good Chardonnay, and not the complex, nuanced wines that fetch top dollar. This would be a big problem, because customers aren’t going to welcome paying a lot of money for wines that are just good varietal wines, rather than great wines of place.

There are of course two aspects to terroir in fine wines. One is the absolute quality potential. Only some sites have the potential to make wines of the very top quality. These places are prized because they make great wines. Whether or not you can taste the place is a secondary issue.

The second is postcode. Great terroirs that express themselves in such a way that you can recognize the place in the wine, or at least some people with the right experience can recognize the place in the wine.

Both aspects of terroir are valid, and both are potentially at risk with climate change.

This brings us to a number of questions. Is the risk real? Yes, it’s getting hot, but Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are still working here. How long will this continue to be the case? We don’t know. One possibility is that altering the viticulture in the region from the way it is currently done in the fancy vineyards (10 000 vines per hectare with a low fruiting wire and low canopy) to the way that it is being done in the less fancy Hautes-Côtes (wider row spacing, higher fruiting wires, bigger canopy) will give some more headroom to the regions. This view was suggested by a wine scientist I interviewed in the region in April when we were filming an episode of The Science of Wine on this topic.

As for switching to other varieties more suited to a warmer climate, this is a very complicated thing to consider. The terroir focus of the region is all about Pinot Noir and Chardonnay expressing the various climats. With new varieties, we might have to start again, and reexamine the climats and their potentials. But with the vast number of growers in the region, and the intricacies of how business is done, this can’t be implemented top down, and grape prices might prevent growers from experimenting with alternatives. There is just too much at stake here to start playing around.

Of course, terroir isn’t owned by Burgundy, and it isn’t restricted solely to France, or solely to the classic regions in the ‘old world’. Other regions will find it easier to experiment and modify their vineyard area with a view to a climatically different future.

Some places are currently climate change winners: Germany and the UK spring to mind. But for most, it is causing problems. Drought and water availability are key issues in many southerly vineyards sites (in the northern hemisphere), and without water you don’t have any terroir!

I think that more emphasis should be made of viticultural shifts that can buy headroom and resilience. Resilient vineyards are going to be very important, because while there are many vintages that are warmer, we are really seeing climate chaos, and some will be wetter, some drier, and some colder. Treating the vineyard as an agroecosystem and encouraging effective biodiversity will really help in this pursuit of resilience.

Ultimately, terroir is a partnership between winegrower and place, and there is a strong human element. Terroir will survive, but it might be a rather different expression of place. Skilled winegrowers will manage to keep place central in their wines even if vintages vary and it’s getting warmer and drier, but only up to a point.

Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

He succeeds Francois van Zyl, who resigned unexpectedly earlier this year, and will take up the role at the Simonsberg property on 1 October. Hailing from a wine farm in Bonnievale in the Western Cape, Van Zyl graduated with a BSc degree in […]

The post Kanonkop appoints Dirk van Zyl as winemaker appeared first on winemag.
content:
Dirk van Zyl.

Kanonkop has appointed Dirk van Zyl, 36, as its new head winemaker. He succeeds Francois van Zyl, who resigned unexpectedly earlier this year, and will take up the role at the Simonsberg property on 1 October.

Hailing from a wine farm in Bonnievale in the Western Cape, Van Zyl graduated with a BSc degree in Viticulture and Oenology from Stellenbosch University in 2012, after which he held the position of winemaker at various Stellenbosch wineries, including Kleine Zalze, De Morgenzon, Saxenburg and, most recently, Glenelly.

Léhandri Bothma will now head up the Glenelly cellar, after three years as assistant winemaker.

title: Melvyn Minnaar: Judging art (and wine)
summary:
Over the years I have had great opportunities to be on the judging side in the visual arts world. Being on a selection panel to rate artworks – like reviewing any creative effort – is an honour, an adventure, a taunt, and a learning experience. A problem facing an art critic or judge is that […]

The post Melvyn Minnaar: Judging art (and wine) appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the years I have had great opportunities to be on the judging side in the visual arts world. Being on a selection panel to rate artworks – like reviewing any creative effort – is an honour, an adventure, a taunt, and a learning experience.

A problem facing an art critic or judge is that astute artists bring on the surprise. They challenge knowledge and experience. One gets face to face with the unfamiliar, the new, the different, the rebellious. And, of course, the brilliance of invention and creativity. A critic should live that long to know and see all!

Same applies to wine, methinks.

A few years ago, I had the exceptional and privileged experience of being included in a panel that was rating the vintage’s young wines for the Hospice de Beaune charity en primeur auction which took place later that year – as usual on the third Sunday in November.

The parallel of the art/wine process and experience is, for me, a delightful mental tickle. So, this was special, and I was wrapped into the delightful dramatics of a bunch of French wine people buzzing around a long table. They were also seemingly having fun while working hard. ‘Fun” hardly comes to mind in the never-ending local arguments about judging wine, sighted or not, scored in petty points or silly stars, and the egos in play.

No, I wasn’t a judge in that French mêlée. Thanks to friends, the lengthy line of knowledgeable winemakers and tasters on duty allowed me to join the circling queue. They drilled around the tasting table at a hair-raising pace. The speed at which they were moving in the line, with me squashed in between, was even more of a challenge than coming to terms with the glorious, pip-squeek but personable, wines. These were hurriedly poured into glasses, swirled, sniffed, thought about, and chucked. Given a nod or not.

What a learning curve it was. Invigorating, it nailed down my life-long love affair with the region and its banner wines.

Besides the cheer, what struck me about the event was the generosity all round. The goodwill towards the Hospice’s cause, long-established since 1859, and heartily supported by the local donated expertise, of course. But also the jolly cellarmasters sharing samples, wisdom, and encouragement – all interacting with the judging process. There was a serious job to be done, but a jollity no one could escape while important decisions were made. (The Hospice de Beaune auction label is as high-status as it gets.)

As art critic, I often experienced similar upbeat merriment among a panel of art judges. And often the consensus, often quickly arrived at, has been an edifying experience: true mastery always proclaims itself. If you look carefully, honestly, and sensitively, it flaunts itself. Isn’t that true for wine as well?

It is impossible to judge art without information and knowledge of provenance.

Years ago, a professor of mine formulated a simple method: look/listen sensitively what the artist wants to tell you. Then, be serious with a good open mind, test that objectively to what you known and have in front of you.

This is one of the reasons why I give short shrift to ‘blind’ wine judging. To me, openness and honesty are the keys in all judging processes. All to often it seems to me that the extraordinary pleasure (and fun) of great wines gets waylaid in one-upmanship judging and a foolish numbers game.

To me the prof’s formula says: know as much as you can of the wine and then judge as open-mindedly and exactly whether it passes the bar it set for itself in the hierarchy of vinous excellence.

Common sense is that artworks do not subscribe to scientific investigating. Yet we establish their excellence and worth. They manage to convey this successfully to us, art observers.

While many components in a glass of wine can be measured scientifically, the overall intention of the winemaker, as you sip his/her creation, is significantly similar to the sensual experience artists expect of an open-minded viewer. Human pleasure, thrill, and intellectual engagement will make itself known.

This is not quantifiable in any system. Just think how ridiculous it will be walking around the Cape Town International Art Fair (coming up again next February) and scoring the paintings, sculptures and videos to a 100-point system.

  • Melvyn Minnaar has written about art and wine for various local and international publications over the years. The creativity that underpins these subjects is an enduring personal passion. He has served on a few “cultural committees”.

content:
Introducing The Cold Soak, a podcast where we discuss what’s been happening in South African wine over the past month – new releases, industry chatter, bold moves and questionable decisions.

Hosted by Ex Animo Wine Co.’s David Clarke and Winemag.co.za editor Christian Eedes, it pairs two informed, independent voices with a clear sense of perspective.

Each episode cuts through the noise: key releases, sharp takes on Winemag reports, and candid discussion on where the industry is headed.

The approach is rigorous but unpretentious, analytical with a touch of humour – equally relevant to industry insiders and engaged drinkers alike.

Listen to the latest review here.

title: New Cape Town spot reimagines the boerewors roll
summary:
Buri, a new casual eatery from Belly Restaurant Group founders Neil Swart and Anouchka Horn, has opened on Harrington Street, Cape Town. The concept reimagines the classic boerewors roll with a custom bun and boerewors developed with Frankie Fenner Meat Merchants. The menu features three boerewors rolls: the Classic with boerewors and fried onions; the […]

The post New Cape Town spot reimagines the boerewors roll appeared first on winemag.
content:
Buri, a new casual eatery from Belly Restaurant Group founders Neil Swart and Anouchka Horn, has opened on Harrington Street, Cape Town. The concept reimagines the classic boerewors roll with a custom bun and boerewors developed with Frankie Fenner Meat Merchants.

The menu features three boerewors rolls: the Classic with boerewors and fried onions; the Farmer with smoor; and the O.G with garlic mayo, chilli chutney and rocket. Once a month, Buri will also introduce a Buri of the Month, giving the team space to showcase different sausages as well as play with different toppings, sauces and combinations.

Other restaurants in the group include Belly of the Beast, Galjoen and Seebamboes.

When excellence becomes widespread, distinction becomes harder. If 15 wines can secure 97 points or higher in a single month, the consumer is left staring at a constellation of high numbers with few navigational tools.

Moreover, the scoring system has its blind spots. A thrilling old-vine Palomino or Colombard can offer rarity, character and a sense of place, yet struggle to reach the mid-90s because it does not conform to the traditional markers of greatness. The Platklip Palomino Old Vine 2025 from Piekenierskloof is a case in point – a wine that gave me much pleasure, but one I could not in good conscience score higher than 93.

There is also a danger that the pursuit of high scores encourages a stylistic consensus. Producers, consciously or otherwise, may gravitate towards the characteristics most consistently rewarded by critics – whether that means power and extraction, or, conversely, extreme reduction, hyper-lean fruit and searing acidity.

As scores climb, so too do the prices attached to benchmark bottles. But does a 98-point wine offer twice the emotional and intellectual reward of a 93-point wine? Rarely. Yet the market treats the numerical gap as a chasm.

When every release is heralded as a “masterpiece” or a “triumph of the vintage,” the language of praise becomes exhausted. Eventually, hyperbole eats its own tail.

The tyranny of the number

Here are some reasons why the growing preoccupation with high scores – and the status they confer – risks narrowing our understanding of what makes a wine important.

The first misconception about wine scores is that they measure how much you will enjoy a wine. They do not.

A score is an assessment of a wine against certain criteria: complexity, balance, intensity, length, typicity, ageing potential and overall quality. It is not a prediction of your personal preference.

A 92-point wine made in a style you love will almost certainly give you more pleasure than a 96-point wine that does not suit your palate. The most important critic remains the person drinking the wine. Some consumers prefer bright, fresh, energetic wines. Others enjoy richness and power. Some want intellectual complexity; others simply want something delicious with dinner. Indeed, even the same person’s preferences legitimately change depending on context, mood and occasion. A score cannot account for all of this.

High-scoring wines are frequently expensive wines. This is understandable. Old vineyards, meticulous farming, limited production and elaborate élevage involving considerable cellar investment all come at a cost.

But the relationship between quality and price is not linear. The difference between a 95-point wine and a 93-point wine may be almost impossible to detect for many consumers, while the price difference can be substantial.

A critic’s most useful recommendation is often not the wine that achieved the highest score, but the wine where quality, character and price intersect most convincingly. A 91-point wine at R150 can be a far more exciting discovery than a 96-point wine at R1,500.

There is a danger that chasing scores turns wine into a trophy-hunting exercise rather than an exploration. I say this with some discomfort, having played my own small part in the 95-point economy. Critics are very much part of the ecosystem that I believe needs to evolve. The highest-scoring wines can become objects of status as much as objects of enjoyment – collected, traded and displayed as markers of taste and access. In this environment, wine risks becoming less about curiosity and pleasure, and more about acquiring the “right” bottles: the rarest, the most expensive, the ones carrying the biggest numbers.

What ever happened to curiosity?

The joy of wine lies partly in finding something unexpected: a producer you have not heard of, a variety you have never tried, a region you have overlooked. Twenty years ago, South Africa’s fine wine consumers were arguably more open-minded and adventurous. The category was still being defined; drinkers were willing to experiment, to follow unfamiliar names and to take a chance on wines that did not yet come with established reputations.

There is a danger that the openness that characterised that era is beginning to narrow. A handful of producers, deservedly admired as they are, have become so firmly entrenched at the top of the wine scene that it becomes harder for newer protagonists to gain attention. The next generation of ambitious producers, or those working with less fashionable varieties and overlooked sites, can struggle to break through.

If every buying decision begins and ends with “What scored highest?”, discovery disappears. And without discovery, wine becomes much less interesting.

The irony is that consumers may need critics more than ever – but perhaps not in the way they once did. The critic’s role is not simply to identify the wines that deserve attention. In an age of abundance, that is no longer enough.

The more valuable role is to provide context. To explain why a wine matters. To identify character and value. To separate the memorable from the merely impressive.

Scores provide a useful common language and a quick reference point. For many consumers, especially those without the time to taste widely, they are an invaluable shortcut. The issue is not their existence, but the weight we attach to them. They should be an invitation to explore, not a reason to stop looking.

There is pleasure in greatness, but there is also pleasure in modesty. Sometimes the most satisfying wine is simply the one that fits the moment. If every bottle we opened had to be “great”, greatness itself would soon lose its meaning.

title: Tim James: Eben Sadie and making wine in the vineyard
summary:
Great wine is made in the vineyard, they say – essentially claiming little more than that you need good grapes for good wine, and the better your grapes the better your wine (as long as you don’t stuff it all up in the winery). Fair enough, but there’s another, more radical way of looking at […]

The post Tim James: Eben Sadie and making wine in the vineyard appeared first on winemag.
content:
Great wine is made in the vineyard, they say – essentially claiming little more than that you need good grapes for good wine, and the better your grapes the better your wine (as long as you don’t stuff it all up in the winery). Fair enough, but there’s another, more radical way of looking at the idea, and Eben Sadie is doing just that, with the multi-varietal wines he makes. The Palladius and Columella blends make for the really complex, fascinating story – one that I think I have come to comprehend, but only recently. A report here, admittedly for the more geekishly inclined.

Let me start the exploration, though, with a few more explanatory words about the two field-blends that I spoke about a few weeks ago when reporting on the latest batch of new releases. Red Songvang and white Twiswind come from two mixed vineyards on the home farm, planted with 12 grapes each (white varieties in the one vineyard, red in the other, obviously). Inevitably they don’t all ripen perfectly at the same time (there does, in fact, seem to be a tendency for such mixed vineyards to start homogenising ripeness  in the longer term). So Eben does two picks in each vineyard, about a week apart, averaging for the earlier- and later-ripening varieties. Then, with no selection except to discard poor quality individual berries, the grapes of the two vineyards will naturally ferment together in their own tanks, and, voilà, the two wines are born and start growing up, heading for the bottle.

As to those youngish vineyards, the plantings in both were informedly experimental. If any of the varieties planted perform somewhat disappointingly or unusefully over the years, they might well be replaced, and, in time, if interplanting is necessary tweaks could be made. The vineyards will evolve, but the concept of expressing the single mixed vineyard will remain: all the varieties unquestioningly accepted and cofermented. Any change to the blend will come from changes in the vineyard.

And so, mutatis mutandis, to the more complexly-treated blends of Palladius (15 varieties off 17 vineyards) and Columella (seven grapes, seven vineyards). I suggested before that they’re perhaps best thought of as field-blends too – with the Swartland serving as an enormous vineyard/tract of terroir to be expressed in all its aspects. A big difference though, is that each of the contributory vineyards is vinified separately. It would be hard to do otherwise but, says Eben, the practice means that the vineyard and how best to manage it can be continuously observed, from year to year (for example, he once came to realise that a particular block was being too heavily composted, with a resultant richness of soil that produced results in the wine that he didn’t want). “I realised”, Eben told me, “that you can’t study a system [that is, Swartland terroir], if you have too many exceptions”.

So, for a year the two sets of wines made from each vineyard mature individually. Then they are blended together according, approximately, to soil type; these going into large foudres for a year – to be further observed – before the final blending is done. I should perhaps say “mixing” rather than “blending”, for the traditional, standard idea of blending wines is for the judicious cellarmaster to sample all the candidate barrels and choose the ones that will make the best wine through quality or character or variety, or perhaps to best continue the established style of the wine. Frequently, as in Bordeaux, the varietal mix of the vineyard is there to allow for the strength of the different varieties in a particular vintage to shine (Cabernet didn’t uniformly ripen, perhaps, but merlot did, or the cab franc performed particularly attractively).

In the Sadie cellar, however, there is no such selection at blending time. There hadn’t even been selection in the vineyards – no picking on two or three different dates to allow for all the grapes to be picked at optimal ripeness; they must all be picked together on the date chosen (a crucial choice, of course). And in the cellar, as I say, no picking and choosing – once the vineyard is picked, its grapes are destined for the final blend and the bottle.

This is a pretty remarkable practice for wines of such ambition (and such reputation and price). Everything is thrown onto the quality of the viticulture, and the selection of vineyards, which of course involves a basic selection of varieties.

Eben has never thought of Columella and Palladius as anything other than works in progress. Over the years they will evolve – primarily through viticultural practice, not in the cellar. We can expect, I think, more vineyards to come into play, rather than any being abandoned while they produce good grapes. Eventually some will die, or need progressive radical interplanting – as is already happening. Some will be tweaked in various ways. Eben tells, for example, of an old chenin vineyard on the home farm that goes into Palladius. He would like more acidity from it, so he’s removing dying or dead vines, replacing them with colombard, clairette and picpoule.

Long ago Eben said to me that “building a great wine is not the work of one generation” – and great Swartland wine is what his ambition and all his efforts are directed towards. He has always serenely accepted that his continuing project will outlast him. More recently he put a slightly different angle on this, talking about what he learns from observing what his component vineyards are offering, year after year, in seasons of different character: “The study of a region”, he says, “is the work of generations”. Even more so in this time of climatic change. Making wine in the vineyard, as done in pre-industrial times, is the hard option.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Jamie Goode: Can terroir survive climate change?
summary:
There’s a lot of discussion about the change in climate. Currently, in the UK, we are in the middle of the hottest summer ever, and the last hottest summer ever was in 2022, just four years ago. It has been like California here: hot and dry, and actually quite pleasant if you like it hot. […]

The post Jamie Goode: Can terroir survive climate change? appeared first on winemag.
content:
There’s a lot of discussion about the change in climate. Currently, in the UK, we are in the middle of the hottest summer ever, and the last hottest summer ever was in 2022, just four years ago. It has been like California here: hot and dry, and actually quite pleasant if you like it hot. But weird, and not the weather usually associated with the UK. Meanwhile, Bordeaux and other more southerly locations have been burning. It’s all a bit apocalyptic.

This brings us round to the notion of terroir. Let’s take Burgundy as an example, which over recent decades has become a place of pilgrimage for wine lovers around the world. In the Parker era, Bordeaux was the pre-eminent wine region; now Parker has stopped and the world has moved away from the somewhat childish tastes of big, ripe, expansive, expensive oak-laden reds and discovered the magic of elegance and place over power, Burgundy is the hallowed ground that wine lovers trek to with reverence and longing.

There are 1,247 climats in Burgundy, on a patchwork of vineyards that threads along 60 km of gentle slopes, running from Dijon to the south of Beaune. These are patches of land recognized as individual terroir units, and together with the hierarchical classification of regional, village, premier cru and grand cru, we have this most beautifully organized presentation of terroir in the world. The status of each parcel tallies well with the soil and underlying geology, as well as the place on the slope. The climats achieved UNESCO world heritage status in 2015.

And these patches of land are then interpreted almost exclusively through the lens of two grape varities: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

But with the change in climate, which has been chaotic, but which has had a clear warming trend, there’s worry that these two remarkable varieties may no longer be faithful conduits of terroir in Burgundy. The fear is that when the climate is changed, the hard work that has led to the identification of these terroirs will begin to unravel.

The theory behind this is that there are windows of terroir expression in terms of grape ripeness. The signal of terroir is lost if the grapes are picked too early, or too late; it is also lost if there is too much ripeness in the grapes, even if they are picked at the right time.

With a warmer climate, there may be vintages where Burgundy from top sites just tastes like good Pinot Noir or good Chardonnay, and not the complex, nuanced wines that fetch top dollar. This would be a big problem, because customers aren’t going to welcome paying a lot of money for wines that are just good varietal wines, rather than great wines of place.

There are of course two aspects to terroir in fine wines. One is the absolute quality potential. Only some sites have the potential to make wines of the very top quality. These places are prized because they make great wines. Whether or not you can taste the place is a secondary issue.

The second is postcode. Great terroirs that express themselves in such a way that you can recognize the place in the wine, or at least some people with the right experience can recognize the place in the wine.

Both aspects of terroir are valid, and both are potentially at risk with climate change.

This brings us to a number of questions. Is the risk real? Yes, it’s getting hot, but Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are still working here. How long will this continue to be the case? We don’t know. One possibility is that altering the viticulture in the region from the way it is currently done in the fancy vineyards (10 000 vines per hectare with a low fruiting wire and low canopy) to the way that it is being done in the less fancy Hautes-Côtes (wider row spacing, higher fruiting wires, bigger canopy) will give some more headroom to the regions. This view was suggested by a wine scientist I interviewed in the region in April when we were filming an episode of The Science of Wine on this topic.

As for switching to other varieties more suited to a warmer climate, this is a very complicated thing to consider. The terroir focus of the region is all about Pinot Noir and Chardonnay expressing the various climats. With new varieties, we might have to start again, and reexamine the climats and their potentials. But with the vast number of growers in the region, and the intricacies of how business is done, this can’t be implemented top down, and grape prices might prevent growers from experimenting with alternatives. There is just too much at stake here to start playing around.

Of course, terroir isn’t owned by Burgundy, and it isn’t restricted solely to France, or solely to the classic regions in the ‘old world’. Other regions will find it easier to experiment and modify their vineyard area with a view to a climatically different future.

Some places are currently climate change winners: Germany and the UK spring to mind. But for most, it is causing problems. Drought and water availability are key issues in many southerly vineyards sites (in the northern hemisphere), and without water you don’t have any terroir!

I think that more emphasis should be made of viticultural shifts that can buy headroom and resilience. Resilient vineyards are going to be very important, because while there are many vintages that are warmer, we are really seeing climate chaos, and some will be wetter, some drier, and some colder. Treating the vineyard as an agroecosystem and encouraging effective biodiversity will really help in this pursuit of resilience.

Ultimately, terroir is a partnership between winegrower and place, and there is a strong human element. Terroir will survive, but it might be a rather different expression of place. Skilled winegrowers will manage to keep place central in their wines even if vintages vary and it’s getting warmer and drier, but only up to a point.

Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

Hailing from a wine farm in Bonnievale in the Western Cape, Van Zyl graduated with a BSc degree in […]

The post Kanonkop appoints Dirk van Zyl as winemaker appeared first on winemag.
content:
Dirk van Zyl.

Kanonkop has appointed Dirk van Zyl, 36, as its new head winemaker. He succeeds Francois van Zyl, who resigned unexpectedly earlier this year, and will take up the role at the Simonsberg property on 1 October.

Hailing from a wine farm in Bonnievale in the Western Cape, Van Zyl graduated with a BSc degree in Viticulture and Oenology from Stellenbosch University in 2012, after which he held the position of winemaker at various Stellenbosch wineries, including Kleine Zalze, De Morgenzon, Saxenburg and, most recently, Glenelly.

Léhandri Bothma will now head up the Glenelly cellar, after three years as assistant winemaker.

title: Melvyn Minnaar: Judging art (and wine)
summary:
Over the years I have had great opportunities to be on the judging side in the visual arts world. Being on a selection panel to rate artworks – like reviewing any creative effort – is an honour, an adventure, a taunt, and a learning experience. A problem facing an art critic or judge is that […]

The post Melvyn Minnaar: Judging art (and wine) appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the years I have had great opportunities to be on the judging side in the visual arts world. Being on a selection panel to rate artworks – like reviewing any creative effort – is an honour, an adventure, a taunt, and a learning experience.

A problem facing an art critic or judge is that astute artists bring on the surprise. They challenge knowledge and experience. One gets face to face with the unfamiliar, the new, the different, the rebellious. And, of course, the brilliance of invention and creativity. A critic should live that long to know and see all!

Same applies to wine, methinks.

A few years ago, I had the exceptional and privileged experience of being included in a panel that was rating the vintage’s young wines for the Hospice de Beaune charity en primeur auction which took place later that year – as usual on the third Sunday in November.

The parallel of the art/wine process and experience is, for me, a delightful mental tickle. So, this was special, and I was wrapped into the delightful dramatics of a bunch of French wine people buzzing around a long table. They were also seemingly having fun while working hard. ‘Fun” hardly comes to mind in the never-ending local arguments about judging wine, sighted or not, scored in petty points or silly stars, and the egos in play.

No, I wasn’t a judge in that French mêlée. Thanks to friends, the lengthy line of knowledgeable winemakers and tasters on duty allowed me to join the circling queue. They drilled around the tasting table at a hair-raising pace. The speed at which they were moving in the line, with me squashed in between, was even more of a challenge than coming to terms with the glorious, pip-squeek but personable, wines. These were hurriedly poured into glasses, swirled, sniffed, thought about, and chucked. Given a nod or not.

What a learning curve it was. Invigorating, it nailed down my life-long love affair with the region and its banner wines.

Besides the cheer, what struck me about the event was the generosity all round. The goodwill towards the Hospice’s cause, long-established since 1859, and heartily supported by the local donated expertise, of course. But also the jolly cellarmasters sharing samples, wisdom, and encouragement – all interacting with the judging process. There was a serious job to be done, but a jollity no one could escape while important decisions were made. (The Hospice de Beaune auction label is as high-status as it gets.)

As art critic, I often experienced similar upbeat merriment among a panel of art judges. And often the consensus, often quickly arrived at, has been an edifying experience: true mastery always proclaims itself. If you look carefully, honestly, and sensitively, it flaunts itself. Isn’t that true for wine as well?

It is impossible to judge art without information and knowledge of provenance.

Years ago, a professor of mine formulated a simple method: look/listen sensitively what the artist wants to tell you. Then, be serious with a good open mind, test that objectively to what you known and have in front of you.

This is one of the reasons why I give short shrift to ‘blind’ wine judging. To me, openness and honesty are the keys in all judging processes. All to often it seems to me that the extraordinary pleasure (and fun) of great wines gets waylaid in one-upmanship judging and a foolish numbers game.

To me the prof’s formula says: know as much as you can of the wine and then judge as open-mindedly and exactly whether it passes the bar it set for itself in the hierarchy of vinous excellence.

Common sense is that artworks do not subscribe to scientific investigating. Yet we establish their excellence and worth. They manage to convey this successfully to us, art observers.

While many components in a glass of wine can be measured scientifically, the overall intention of the winemaker, as you sip his/her creation, is significantly similar to the sensual experience artists expect of an open-minded viewer. Human pleasure, thrill, and intellectual engagement will make itself known.

This is not quantifiable in any system. Just think how ridiculous it will be walking around the Cape Town International Art Fair (coming up again next February) and scoring the paintings, sculptures and videos to a 100-point system.

  • Melvyn Minnaar has written about art and wine for various local and international publications over the years. The creativity that underpins these subjects is an enduring personal passion. He has served on a few “cultural committees”.
